exam: A 7‑year‑old with severe malaria has a GCS of 9 – what immediate step addresses oxidative injury? — Give IV artesunate promptly; consider adjunctive vitamin C/E if labs show high MDA, but do not delay antimalarial therapy.

A sickle‑cell patient presents with chest pain and rising LDH – how does oxidative stress influence your differential? — Recognise ROS‑mediated vaso‑occlusion; prioritize analgesia, oxygen, and consider exchange transfusion if organ damage progresses.
In a patient with G6PD deficiency and jaundice, why is oxidative stress relevant and which drug must be avoided? — Oxidative stress precipitates hemolysis; avoid sulfonamides and primaquine.

A TB meningitis case shows high CSF protein and low glucose – how might oxidative stress affect prognosis? — Elevated ROS correlates with neuronal injury; aggressive anti‑TB therapy and adjunctive steroids are indicated.

When serum lactate is unavailable, how can you assess severe oxidative stress in sepsis? — Use clinical perfusion markers (cold extremities, capillary refill >3 seconds) and urine output; treat sepsis early.

Why is routine high‑dose vitamin E not recommended in HIV patients despite oxidative stress? — Long‑term high‑dose vitamin E increases risk of hemorrhagic stroke; use standard doses only if deficiency is proven.

A patient on chronic antiretroviral therapy develops elevated MDA – what does this indicate and how should you respond? — Ongoing oxidative injury despite viral suppression; optimise nutrition, consider antioxidant supplementation, and review drug interactions.
How does oxidative stress contribute to acute kidney injury in severe malaria, and what preventive measure is key? — ROS damage renal tubules; maintain adequate hydration and avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
ai.title: Oxidative Stress in Clinical Medicine
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Oxidative stress reflects an imbalance between reactive oxygen species and antioxidant defenses, contributing to tissue injury in many common tropical diseases. Recognising its clinical clues guides diagnosis, risk stratification and supportive management.

b: Key ROS: superoxide anion, hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radical
Major antioxidants: SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, vitamins A/E/C
sections.p: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are normal by‑products of metabolism. When production exceeds the capacity of enzymatic (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase) and non‑enzymatic (vitamin C, E, glutathione) antioxidants, oxidative stress occurs, damaging lipids, proteins and DNA.

b: Lipid peroxidation → membrane fragility, measured by malondialdehyde (MDA)
sections.p: Oxidative stress is a pathophysiological mechanism, not a disease. It amplifies injury in infections (malaria, TB, HIV), haemolytic disorders (sickle cell), chronic liver disease, and drug‑induced toxicity.

b: Severe malaria: high plasma MDA predicts cerebral involvement
Sickle cell vaso‑occlusive crisis: elevated ROS correlates with pain severity
TB meningitis: oxidative markers linked to neurologic decline
sections.p: Patients present with non‑specific signs of organ dysfunction; the clue is a disease known to generate ROS. In low‑resource settings, oxidative stress worsens outcomes of malaria, severe sepsis, and sickle‑cell crises.

t.b: Is oxidative lipid damage present? Elevated MDA supports high ROS burden; if unavailable, rely on clinical severity scores.
Are antioxidant reserves depleted? Low GSH suggests need for supportive antioxidants; if lab not available, consider empirical vitamin C/E in severe cases.

b: Link oxidative stress to organ‑specific signs (e.g., jaundice from hemolysis, neuro‑deficits in cerebral malaria).
Prioritise management: treat underlying infection first, then consider antioxidant therapy.
sections.p: Examiners test integration of pathophysiology with bedside decisions, especially in resource‑limited contexts.

b: Confusing elevated ROS markers with bacterial infection.
Assuming antioxidant supplements cure malaria or TB.
sections.p: Students often treat oxidative stress as a primary diagnosis or prescribe high‑dose antioxidants without indication.
Focus on tests that confirm the underlying disease and, when possible, quantify oxidative damage.

t.b: Is hemolysis occurring? Low hemoglobin with high retics suggests oxidative hemolysis (e.g., G6PD deficiency).
Is tissue hypoxia driving ROS? Elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L) indicates severe metabolic stress.

b: Antimicrobial therapy for malaria (artesunate), TB (rifampicin‑based regimen), HIV (ART).
Avoid drugs that further increase ROS (e.g., high‑dose paracetamol in liver disease).
sections.p: Treat the precipitating cause, support antioxidant capacity, and monitor organ function.
